text: Santa Rosa de Osos is a middle city and municipality in northern Antioquia, Colombia, bordered on the north by Yarumal and Angostura, on the east by Guadalupe and Carolina del Principe, on the south by Donmatías, San Pedro de los Milagros, and Entrerríos, and on the west by Belmira and San José de la Montaña. Before the Spanish arrival, the indigenous Nutabes lived in the area, known for their agility, craftsmanship in cotton, and gold extraction, with a patriarchal society and beliefs in life after death, where the dead were buried with utensils, jewelry, food, and clothing. In 1541, Spanish conquistador Francisco Vallejo discovered the region, naming it "Valley of the Bears" due to the abundance of bears, and by 1600, gold was found in abundance. In 1636, Captain Antonio Serrano y Espejo led a group of settlers to establish a settlement on the site, approved by King Philip IV of Spain. In 1659, the area became a parish under Bishop Jacinto Vasco de Contreras y Velarde and was renamed "San Jacinto de los Osos." In 1792, it was renamed "Villa de Nuestra Señora de Chiquinquirá de los Osos," and in 1811, it acquired its current name, Santa Rosa de Osos. It was officially established as a municipality in 1814 by dictator Juan del Corral. In 1917, the Diocese of Santa Rosa de Osos was created by Pope Benedicto XV, with investment from the Yarce Betancur family, one of the most powerful families at the time and founders of a local school. Bishop Miguel Angel Builes Gomez, appointed in 1924, led the diocese for over forty years and founded four religious communities: the Sisters Teresitas Comtemplativas, Teresitas Missionary Sisters, the Daughters of Our Lady of Mercy, and the Xaverian Yarumal Missionaries. Currently, Bishop Jorge Alberto Ossa Soto oversees the diocese. The municipality is known as "The City Religious" due to its strong Catholic heritage and religious tourism, featuring the Cathedral, chapels, and monuments reflecting the devotion of its people. Santa Rosa is a major producer of milk and water for the Aburrá Valley metropolitan area, supporting the construction of Lakes Riogrande I and II. Marshal Jorge Robledo arrived in Anzá in September 1541 and sent commissions, including one led by Francisco Vallejo to the "Llanos de Ovejas" (modern San Pedro de los Milagros and Entrerríos), where he discovered a cold valley named "Bear's Valley." The Nutabes resisted Spanish presence, leading Vallejo to abandon the area due to hostilities, and the region was considered poor and unprofitable, remaining neglected for nearly a century despite visits by Don Andres De Valdivia and Don Gaspar De Rodas in the mid-16th century. Early colonization began with Pedro Gutierrez Colmenero (first mayor of Medellín, 1675) and Don Antonio De Mesa, and Juan Nuño De Sotomayor discovered minerals in 1645, beginning operations in streams such as San Juan, La Trinidad, Orobajo, San Jose, San Antonio, Santa Ana, and San Lorenzo, as well as the Guadalupe River and Los Martires stream. Gutierrez Colmenero worked the mines, while Fernando Toro Zapata operated the Caruquia stream. The first village was located south of the current city, now the Arenales neighborhood, called La Rancheria in the 18th century, owned by Captain Ignacio Velez De Rivero and featuring a chapel built in 1740, linked to Catholic tradition. Rich mineral deposits near the Bramadora, San Juan, and San Antonio streams attracted many people when Antioquia's gold declined; by 1650, there were over 700 Black people and more than 500 Spaniards or their descendants working in mining, many of whom were wealthy. Mining processes were improved by Mon and Velarde, who established mining laws, and by Monsieur Laneret or Moneret, who introduced water-powered mills in the late 17th century. In the early 18th century, large immigration from Medellín and Rionegro increased the population, leading to the name change to San Jacinto de los Osos by 1770. The first priest was Juan Bautista Dávila Knight, though earlier residents included Pedro Martin de Mora and Fray Pedro Simon, who wrote about the mines. During the 18th century, five chapels existed outside the parish, including Tierradentro, and the parish chapel was dedicated to Our Lady of Guadalupe, commemorating a miracle involving Spanish adventurer Pedro Bustamante, who, harassed by natives, prayed to the Virgin and was saved by Juan Torres, who later died under attack from a native, with his body appearing to soldiers at the funeral—this story may have inspired the name Guadalupe River, though no definitive historical evidence confirms it. The village cemetery was located where today's Simon Bolivar Park, the main square, and was constructed with help from Don Pedro Rodriguez de Zea in 1775, who was governor of Los Osos and authorized the creation of Yarumal, Don Matías, and Carolina del Principe. A hidden history involves severe discrimination against Black people; despite Antioquia being one of the first regions to grant freedom to slaves, the valley remained harsh, with cruel treatment by Spaniards. Notably, Don Juan Jose Salazar and María del Pardo were known for whipping slaves and chaining them, and also for flaying cows and killing cattle in extreme pain. Salazar, who worked in the La Trinidad mine and in the area now known as Gómez Plata, was nicknamed "The Sombrerón" for wearing a large hat; after his death, residents believed he wandered through the town nightly with two large dogs, a belief that became a popular urban legend and is remembered in a street in Hoyorrico. In 1792, Governor Francisco Baraya and La Campa established the Villa, named "Village of Our Lady of the Rosary of Chiquinquirá of the Bears," marking a new mining boom with new wealthy entrepreneurs like Zulaibar replacing old elites and forming economically and culturally significant companies. Scientific advances in gold mining, especially in lode mines like Las Cruces and Las Animas, brought high returns, but gold declined quickly, leading to a shift to agriculture and livestock, improving living conditions and transforming the region into a green city with over 100 consecutive years of environmental stability and economic prosperity. The name "Santa Rosa de Osos" honors Santa Rosa de Lima and the spectacled bears that once abounded in the region. The municipality has a good population projection, driving urban development with new neighborhoods and demolition of old houses, expanding its urban perimeter and planning residential projects with services, though road and public space issues persist due to increased traffic and poor maintenance, with many streets, avenues, and parks in disrepair and lacking a central park. Public monuments and furniture such as benches, lamps, and waste bins are damaged by vandalism and neglect. Parks include those in the city and districts. Santa Rosa has a transport terminal with offices for various carriers and social services, offering daily public routes to all districts and villages, as well as to San José de la Montaña, Entrerríos, San Pedro de los Milagros, Don Matías, Carolina del Principe, and Medellín, with frequent service. Sports infrastructure includes three covered coliseums: CIC El Alto de La Mina, Minor, and Antonio Roldan Betancur, a municipal synthetic grass court, an athletic complex with a track, bicicross track, tennis court, and over 10 multisport covered courts across neighborhoods, plus open-air facilities. In Riogrande, Alto de La Mina, and St. Thomas Aquinas Seminary, there are well-equipped soccer fields. The city has excellent hotel infrastructure with diverse amenities and numerous museums, monuments, and historical buildings alongside its many churches. With a population of 36,063, the municipality has a primary care hospital and three health institutions (IPS): MEDICAL CENTER SANTA ROSA DE OSOS LTDA., CIMA HEADQUARTERS NORTH—San Juan de Dios Hospital, and IPS NORTH SAN MARCOS DE LEON S.A.S. The municipality has UNE-EDATEL for fixed telephony and internet, with excellent mobile coverage from Claro, Movistar, and Tigo. Two local radio stations, "Radio Más" and "Radio Mi Tierra," provide local information. CAPSOS, a local television company, offers over 60 channels across genres, aiming to meet community needs for information, education, and entertainment, reflecting cultural identity and creating audiovisual memory of santarosan history. It provides spaces for community voice and alternative development. In rural areas, DIRECTV is the primary television service. Electricity is provided by EPM throughout the municipality, with good public lighting coverage. The urban center has a modern domestic gas network from EPM. Water and sewer services are managed by Sustainable Water Supply and Sewerage S.A. (AASSA), with extensive drinking water coverage from the Chichi and Agua Mala (Tenche River source) streams, fed by gravity from Cerro San José and pumped from Las Cruces, forming an efficient aqueduct. Sewer systems have weaknesses: some areas lack networks and discharge directly into water sources, with community septic tanks in many places; urban streams suffer from pollution, especially Agüitas Claras, which receives 55% of untreated urban wastewater from sectors like El Hoyo, 33, Villa Cruz, and others, flowing into the Bramadora stream, and 45% goes to the Guadalupe River—12% to the Portal stream, which flows into San Jose, and 33% directly into the Guadalupe River in areas like Barro Blanco, Los Chorros, and El Turco. Wastewater from the Guadalupe River is collected by a system that reaches the Turco wastewater treatment plant, which operates within acceptable pollution standards but still visibly affects the river. Rural districts and villages have community-managed aqueducts, with basic sanitation provided by the mayor and septic tanks meeting quality standards. Some farms use water concessions or stream deposits for domestic use. The population was estimated at 37,864 in 2020, 36,103 in 2016 (19,012 urban, 17,091 rural), and literacy was 91.3% in 2005. According to DANE's 2005 census, the ethnographic composition of the municipality is detailed. The municipality has five official districts: Aragon, Hoyorrico, San Pablo, Riogrande, and San Isidro; Caney is awaiting official district status through a pending PBOT update. It has over 72 rural villages. Santa Rosa de Osos is located in the northern highlands with an average elevation of 2,550 meters above sea level, with steep slopes in San Pablo and San Isidro where elevation drops sharply to warmer thermal zones. Its total area is 812 square kilometers, of which 805 are rural and 7 urban. The territorial size is slightly larger than Kiribati and over 400 times the surface of Monaco.
